title: Perspectives on inverse design for AI magnonics
authors: Franz Vilsmeier, Florian Bruckner, Claas Abert, Dieter Suess, Andrii V. Chumak
abstract: Inverse design - specifying a desired functionality and letting a computational algorithm find the optimal structure - has emerged as a powerful paradigm for magnonic device engineering. In this article, we survey the rapidly growing field of inverse-design magnonics, organising it along two axes: the design variables (topology, material parameters, and magnetic field landscape) and the algorithmic toolbox (gradient-free, gradient-based, and neural-network-based methods) together with the differentiable micromagnetic solvers that enable them. We then identify open frontiers that we consider most promising for the next phase of the field: sensitivity analysis and robust design to bridge the gap between simulation and experiment; input shaping and transducer optimisation; the incorporation of nonlinear spin-wave effects as an explicit design resource; spatially structured amplification; self-adapting media and machine-learning-based design; and the long-term vision of a universal, reconfigurable magnonic platform. We argue that magnonics and artificial intelligence are converging from two directions - machine-learning tools for designing magnonic devices, and magnonic devices as hardware for neuromorphic computation - and propose the term AI magnonics to describe this emerging paradigm.
summary: This paper surveys the rapidly growing field of inverse design for magnonic devices, treating it as a powerful paradigm shift from traditional engineering. It organizes the research by design variables and computational algorithms, proposing 'AI magnonics' to describe the synergy between machine learning tools and magnetic hardware for advanced applications like neuromorphic computing.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a systematic, computational framework for designing magnonic devices by specifying desired functionalities and allowing an algorithm to determine the optimal physical structure.
main_result: The authors propose 'AI magnonics' as the emerging paradigm describing the convergence of machine learning tools for device design and magnonic devices used for neuromorphic computation.
method: The review surveys inverse design techniques, categorizing them by design variables (topology, material parameters, field landscape) and algorithmic toolboxes (gradient-free, gradient-based, NN-based methods).
model_or_system: The system under study is magnonics, which involves spin waves propagating in magnetic thin films. The physics is governed by the nonlinear Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert (LLG) equation.
key_observables: Spin-wave response, filter characteristics, logic gate operation, and pattern recognition capability.
important_parameters: Design variables include topology ($ho$), material parameters ($M_s, K_u, \alpha$), and the external magnetic field landscape ($B_{ext}(x, y)$).
main_assumptions: The work assumes that inverse design can overcome the limitations of intuition-guided, direct device engineering.
figures_summary: Figure 1 contrasts direct vs. inverse design workflows; Figure 2 schematically maps out the five key design variables (Topology, Material parameters, Field landscape, Input shaping, Nonlinear effects); Table 2 organizes literature by optimization class and variable type.
paper_structure: The paper is structured as a comprehensive survey, first defining the problem via direct vs. inverse design, then systematically organizing the field along two axes: design variables and algorithmic toolboxes, before concluding with open frontiers and proposing the 'AI magnonics' concept.
why_interesting: While focused on classical magnetism, the methodology heavily relies on integrating advanced computational optimization (gradient-based methods) with physical systems, mirroring techniques used in designing quantum circuits or simulating complex many-body Hamiltonians where parameter space exploration is key.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Inverse design as a paradigm shift in magnonics. Both workflows share the same three elements—a set of specifications, a device geometry, and a target performance (shown as a dartboard). (a) In direct design, a researcher converts the specifications into a geometry guided by physical intuition, and the resulting performance is only evaluated afterwards, with no guarantee that it meets the target (the dart may miss). (b) In inverse design, the target performance is instead prescribed up front and an optimisation algorithm works backward to the device geometry (note the reversed arrow), reliably reaching the target, often through non-intuitive geometries that outperform...

Figure 2. Design variables in inverse-design magnonics. From left to right: topology (binary or level-set material distribution), material parameters (spatially varying Ms, Ku, α), and magnetic field landscape (reconfigurable stray-field or current-loop patterns) constitute the three established design variables. Input shaping (excitation waveforms and antenna geometry) and nonlinear effects (frequency shifts or multi-magnon interactions as a design resource) are discussed as open perspectives in Sec. 4.

Figure 3. The algorithmic toolbox of inverse-design magnonics. (a) Gradient-free methods evaluate a population of candidate designs (grey) directly, iteratively converging on the best candidate found (red) without using any derivative information—for example direct binary search [24], genetic algorithms, and direct search [32]. (b) Gradient-based methods follow the gradient of the objective downhill across a non-convex landscape, converging to a minimum (red) while risking entrapment in local minima; examples include the adjoint method [27] and backpropagation through a differentiable solver [25,30,31]. Figure 4. AI magnonics: the convergence of inverse design and neuromorphic magnonics. In the emerging AI magnonics paradigm, the two fields converge from two directions—machine- learning tools design the device, while the magnonic spin-wave medium itself performs neuromorphic computation, depicted here as two interpenetrating lobes—an artificial neural network and a propagating spin-wave medium—that meet and fuse at the point where the two disciplines converge (from AI-designed magnonics to magnonic hardware for AI ).
